title: Om

teacherSummary.text: Still aching for his son, Siddhartha sees his reflection resemble his own father and understands the circle of suffering. He confesses everything to Vasudeva, who leads him to listen; the river's voices—joy and sorrow, good and evil—blend into one word, Om. Siddhartha achieves serenity. Vasudeva, his work done, walks into the forest to die.

vocabulary.definition: The flower of a plant, or the essential organs of reproduction, with their appendages
vocabulary.context: Slowly blossomed, slowly ripened in Siddhartha the realisation, the knowledge, what wisdom actually was, what the goal of his long search was.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: Having the power of serving or accomplishing fate
vocabulary.context: Was it not a comedy, a strange and stupid matter, this repetition, this running around in a fateful circle?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: A vessel for conveying passengers, merchandise, etc., across streams and other narrow waters
vocabulary.context: He no longer used the ferryboat, his eyes were starting to get weak, and not just his eyes; his arms and hands as well.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: Slowly blossomed, slowly ripened in Siddhartha the realisation, the knowledge, what wisdom actually was, what the goal of his long search was.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: To hinder from freedom of thought, speech, or action by something which impedes or confuses mental action
vocabulary.context: He reported everything, he was able to say everything, even the most embarrassing parts, everything could be said, everything shown, everything he could tell.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: The act of nourishing or nursing
vocabulary.context: But the wound still burned, longingly and bitterly Siddhartha thought of his son, nurtured his love and tenderness in his heart, allowed the pain to gnaw at him, committed all foolish acts of love.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: One who, or that which, flees from danger, duty, restraint, etc.; a fugitive
vocabulary.context: He presented his wound, also told how he fled today, how he ferried across the water, a childish runaway, willing to walk to the city, how the river had laughed.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: It still resounded, full of suffering, searching, but other voices joined it, voices of joy and of suffering, good and bad voices, laughing and sad ones, a hundred voices, a thousand voices.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: Act of taking a bath or baths
vocabulary.context: To show his wound to this listener was the same as bathing it in the river, until it had cooled and become one with the river.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: The act of one who, or that which, weaves
vocabulary.context: Vasudeva was sitting in the hut and weaving a basket.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

context.history: Hesse blends Hindu and Buddhist ideas of unity with Western mysticism.

significance: The climax: all opposites unite into one harmony, and the student becomes the master.
discussionQuestions: What does Siddhartha finally understand when he hears all the voices together?

How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the search for self-knowledge?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Om,” how does Hesse show hearing the many voices? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the symbolism you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Om develops the idea of hearing the many voices. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of symbolism and imagery shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Hermann Hesse uses symbolism in Om to complicate the reader's understanding of hearing the many voices. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Om within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of hearing the many voices responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Om as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of hearing the many voices. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Siddhartha.

satQuestions.passage: Slowly blossomed, slowly ripened in Siddhartha the realisation, the knowledge, what wisdom actually was, what the goal of his long search was. It was nothing but a readiness of the soul, an ability, a secret art, to think every moment, while living his life, the thought of oneness, to be able to feel and inhale the oneness. Slowly this blossomed in him, was shining back at him from Vasudeva’s old, childlike face: harmony, knowledge of the eternal perfection of the world, smiling, oneness.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Om”?
options: Injustice and the burden of silence
Obsession and the discovery of life

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: What does Siddhartha finally understand when he hears all the voices together? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include blossomed, fateful, ferryboat, ripened, embarrassing. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “Slowly blossomed, slowly ripened in Siddhartha the realisation, the knowledge, what wisdom actually was, what the goal of his long search was.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: The flower of a plant, or the essential organs of reproduction, with their appendages.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Siddhartha would have known. Hesse blends Hindu and Buddhist ideas of unity with Western mysticism. Now, why does this chapter matter? The climax: all opposites unite into one harmony, and the student becomes the master. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Symbolism, Imagery, Theme.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot symbolism, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
segments.passage: Slowly blossomed, slowly ripened in Siddhartha the realisation, the knowledge, what wisdom actually was, what the goal of his long search was. It was nothing but a readiness of the soul, an ability, a secret art, to think every moment, while living his life, the thought of oneness, to be able to feel and inhale the oneness. Slowly this blossomed in him, was shining back at him from Vasudeva’s old, childlike face: harmony, knowledge of the eternal perfection of the world, smiling, oneness.
